nameStory: This hardy little lichen gets its "snow-bed" name from its ability to thrive in places where snow lingers late into spring and summer. The "Iceland" part reflects its Arctic origins and love of cold, harsh conditions that remind it of the frigid landscapes near the polar regions. It's like nature's own snow-loving survivalist!
description: Snow-bed Iceland Lichen is a small, leafy lichen that forms neat rosettes or irregular patches on rocks and soil in New England's highest, coldest spots. The individual lobes are narrow and finger-like, typically grayish-green to brownish, and the whole patch rarely exceeds a few inches across. This tough little survivor looks almost like tiny lettuce leaves that have been freeze-dried, with a distinctly leathery texture when you gently touch it. It's one of our rarest lichens, found only in the most extreme mountain environments.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms small rosettes or irregular patches with narrow, finger-like lobes that radiate outward from the center, feeling leathery and somewhat stiff to the touch

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-green to brownish when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet, with darker undersides that are often blackish

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches typically 1-3 inches across, with lobes that are narrow (2-4mm wide) and relatively short

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Grows on acidic rocks, thin soil, and sometimes directly on gravelly ground in exposed mountain locations

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Upper surface feels smooth to slightly rough, never powdery or bumpy, with a somewhat waxy quality when fresh

habitat: This rare lichen is found only in New England's most extreme alpine and subalpine environments, particularly on Mount Washington and other high peaks above 3,500 feet elevation. Look for it in areas where snow persists late into summer, often growing on exposed acidic bedrock, thin gravelly soils, or in rocky crevices where moisture collects. It thrives in the harshest spots where few other plants can survive the brutal winter winds and short growing seasons.

seasonality.spring: Often still buried under snow in its high-elevation haunts. When exposed, appears dull and contracted from winter's harsh conditions.
seasonality.summer: At its most visible and colorful when briefly free from snow cover. This is the best time to spot its characteristic growth form.
seasonality.fall: Begins to look more subdued as it prepares for the long winter ahead. Still identifiable but less vibrant in color.
seasonality.winter: Usually completely buried under deep snow for months, essentially dormant and invisible to observers.

funFact: This lichen can survive being frozen solid for up to 8 months of the year and actually needs those extreme freeze-thaw cycles to thrive - it's so adapted to harsh conditions that it would struggle to survive in your backyard garden!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small foliose lichens in alpine areas, but its narrow, finger-like lobes and preference for the most extreme exposed sites help distinguish it. Remember: if you can easily hike to it without serious mountain gear, it's probably not Snow-bed Iceland Lichen!
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it's from Iceland, this lichen is actually found across Arctic and alpine regions of the Northern Hemisphere. The extreme rarity in New England (only 2 recorded observations) makes every sighting scientifically valuable - if you think you've found it, definitely photograph it and report the location to local naturalist groups.
compareHints: Since it's the only Cetrariella species in our region, compare it to other small alpine lichens in the shield lichen family. Unlike the more common Cetraria lichens, Snow-bed Iceland Lichen has narrower, more delicate-looking lobes and grows in smaller, more compact patches. It lacks the rolled or channeled leaf edges that many similar mountain lichens display.
